In August, 1923, the rate to Port Colbome was 3.33, as against the same rate for the year 1922. In September the rate was even lower in 1923 than it was in 1922.
Oh, no.

November I should have said; was lower; the rate was slightly higher in September 1923-only 1 of a cent. The rate in 1922 was 3.72 as against 3.99 for 1923, a very, very slight difference. In August the rates were exactly the same. In the month of October there was a difference of only one-quarter of a cent. In the month of November the rates were half a cent lower in 1923 than in 1922.
The act was gone then.

Taking the whole season of
1922 as against the whole season of 1923, there was a difference of two-thirds of a cent a bushel. To Georgian bay ports there was a difference during the whole season of one-tenth of a cent a bushel.

In September
last, were not the Duluth-Buffalo rates from 21 to 2f cents a bushel? Does my hon. friend deny that?
I have not the American rates before me. I am more interested in the Canadian rates.

I can quite
understand why he would not have the American rates, where 62 per cent of the whole movement went. I am going to ask my hon. friend another question. Will he deny this fact, and it is a fact, that on September 20th the Fort William-Buffalo rate was 5 cents?
During the month of September the rate averaged 4.57 cents.

That was going up pretty well. My hon. friend corroborates me pretty well, I think; 4.58 as against 21 and 2f; that is the only harm, according to my hon. friend, the act did. Will he deny this, that in October the Fort William-Buffalo rate reached 61 cents?
It may have reached that, but the average was 5.24.

Are you sure
of that?
Quite positive.
He will not deny that it reached 61, but it averaged 5.24 for the month, as against 3 cents Duluth-Buffalo. That is going up pretty well. Does my hon. friend deny the Duluth-Buffalo rate was 3 cents?

I have already said that I have not the Duluth-Buffalo rates before me.
Supply-Canada Grain Act
There is just the loss on the great majority of the movement.
If I had those rates before me I might find they were just as inaccurate as the figures my hon. friend has just quoted.

The figures I
have quoted are not wrong Mr. Chairman. So far my hon. friend has not said one is wrong. What is the use of insinuating that any of them is wrong when he cannot deny one of them? He said a moment ago he could not tell whether the rate had reached 6| cents for the month; he could only say the average was so and so, and the average was bad enough.

I have given you the figures
from Canadian ports to Canadian ports.

What is to be
done about it?

There is one matter I would like to bring to the minister's attention. The total cost of handling 1,000 bushels at Port Colborne is given here as 4.35 cents, and for handling 1,000 bushels at Buffalo 14.70 cents. That is a very great advantage on handling charges in favour of Canadian boats carrying grain to Canadian ports. Has that matter been looked into?
No, but the ex-Minister of Finance will be able to answer that.

It shows a very great advantage in favour of the Canadian boats in handling charges. I was surprised at the attempt the minister made to-night to show that there were no high rates for carrying wheat during the fall of 1923. Those who ship early in the season found it a serious matter. They had to pay very high charges at that time. Of course matters were not so bad when the minister made arrangements whereby American boats could carry Canadian grain; but we know from experience what the charges were in the early part of the season.
But the facts do not bear out the statement of my hon. friend from West York. The rates were only very slightly higher.
Probably on the average.

On the average during the
month.
But if you had happened to be one of the early shippers that would not have done you much good.

Why did the minister
ibrogate the act? He had no right to, it was a straight piece of autocracy.

He did not abrogate the act.
He accepted the interpretation of the chairman of the Canadian Grain Board.

The interpretation was
that there was no act.

My right hon. friend knows
that lawyers differ. Because he holds one view is no reason why another member of the bar should not hold an entirely different view.

I suppose not, but no
lawyer nor no human being ever held the view that the hon. minister gave. He does not hold it himself. He knows that the act was the most costly blunder and piece of humbug that was ever put through this House. It was not as big a humbug as the Wheat Board but it was just as big a blunder -just a stupid, costly blunder. He as a business man saw that he had to get some way to extricate himself from the hole in which he found himself, and he took this round about way of getting an interpretation. Everybody laughed at it; the minister is laughing at it himself-the putting of an interpretation on a clause in the act. Now, what is the minister going to do? Why does he not come here and repeal the act and tell the House the government made the mistake which they know they did make?

I believe that what has
been said about the act being rather immature and not being sufficiently considered last session is perfectly correct. I believe also that the resistance shown by the vessel owners did cause a raise in rates in the early part of the season; but I think some of the figures that have been given are rather misleading. We all know that in the month of September, when very little grain is passing down the lakes, our Canadian rates are low, lower than later on.

Does the hon.
gentleman know the tonnage moving in September?
I have not the figures by months, but I can give the average for the year.
But the figures by the month are the figures that count. It is something like twenty-four millions.

The figures for the calendar year and the figures for the crop year are entirely different. One needs to know what set of figures he is comparing. It may be of interest for the purpose of comparison to give the rate for 1915. The average rate from Fort

Supply-Canada Grain Act
William to Port Colbome in that year was 1.71. The average rate for 1922 was 4.05 and for the calendar year it was 3.81. For the calendar year 1923 the average was 4.24, so that while the rate may have been higher in certain months the variation was not very great.
I may say that while this controversy was going on I sent a wire to the minister suggesting that he intercede with the railways in order to have the all-rail rate from Armstrong to Quebec lowered. I have never been able to understand why the rate from Armstrong, directly north of Fort William, to the city of Quebec, a distance of 960 miles, is 21 cents. That used to be the figure and I believe it is still. Let me point out to the minister that if grain were carried from Armstrong to the city of Quebec at the same rate it is now carried from Calgary to Fort William the figure would be 11 cents. Now, when we have built this railway at enormous expense-with a road bed that is excellent and a grade that is good

and when we have a terminal in the city of Quebec with an elevator capacity of 2,000,000 bushels, that was at this time only partly occupied, why should the railway rate be prohibitive? It would be wise, if such a difficulty occurs again and the shippers are determined and defiant, for the minister to take steps to set aside and suspend the coasting laws. I knew when I sent this wire to the minister the proposition would be only a partial remedy, for the reason that even if the rates on the railway were lowered at once the rolling stock would be lacking; it would not be possible to get sufficient rolling stock to carry any very great quantity of grain down to Quebec.
One thought I should like to express is this:	The minister has been severely criticised for interceding with the American and Canadian shippers, and it has been suggested that he practically invited them to break the Canadian law. I do not feel like seriously condemning the minister for that course because grain was coming down from Winnipeg at the rate of a trainload of forty cam every thirty minutes, night and day. You can see what that meant. For that grain to be tied up, even for a week or a month, meant enormous loss. Therefore I would rather approve the course the minister took, even if he had to pocket his dignity for the time being, in order that he might save that enormous loss. I did not at that time, and I do not now, feel like seriously condemning the minister, even if he took this-I will not say undignified course, for it was rather a
case of bottling his pride I suppose. It has been spoken of as rather ridiculous by some hon.. members, but considering the enormous amount that was at stake and the financial condition of those who would suffer, those who were growing grain, I was glad the minister took any steps that might be necessary in order to permit the grain to proceed down the lakes. I shall not attempt to discuss this matter very fully because later on when the Welland canal estimates are being considered I shall deal with the question of the freight rates and the reason why Canadian grain passes through American channels to the extent that it does.

I do not understand how my hon. friend, from Brandon (Mr. Forke) could interpret my remarks as an attempt to justify the rates in force on the lakes last fall or at any time. I was simply endeavouring to point out to the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) that the rates last fall, or during the shipping season in 1923, were not higher than they were in 1922.
My hon. friend from Saltcoats (Mr. Sales), made some reference to the marketing of grain. I wish to say that there is no subject occupying my mind more than that of trying to work out some plan that will permit the marketing of the grain of the Canadian West at a lower cost than is the case at the present time. My hon. friend has apparently jumped to a conclusion. He made the remark that I had been carrying on negotiations with the ocean vessel owners and had apparently been unable to accomplish anything. I want to inform my hon. friend that it is true I have been carrying on negotiations regarding ocean freight rates on cattle, but before this session is closed I hope to work out some solution that will lessen the cost very materially of carrying the cattle from Canadian ports to English ports.

I would like to say in explanation that I was not exactly blaming the minister; in fact I agree to some extent with the remarks of the hon. member for Saltcoats (Mr. Sales); but what did vex me last fall was that there seemed to be a trial of strength between the Canadian government and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and something had to be done. I think probably the minister took the proper steps and I would like to see this government and Canada in such a position that no group of shipowners could dictate just exactly what is to take place on the Great Lakes, a result that could be brought about by abrogating the coastal laws.
Supply-Canada Grain Act

I was glad to have the assurance of the minister that this question of securing lower transportation for our grain is occupying a good deal of his attention; but still I am not quite satisfied with the way the coastal laws are being handled. I agree that when we have a club it should be used, and if this were used! as a club at the proper time, we would not be asking for the repeal of the coastal laws. That is the whole issue at stake. If the government were prepared to use it at the critical time it would be all right. But the reason we object to the very existence of the coastal laws is that it is only at long periods that this weapon is ever used at all. The minister said himself that competition was one of the things that regulated freight rates. We had a very good proof of this in the insurance rates. I think the government felt that the practice of vessel owners handling insurance was wrong, and it was done away with. As a result I see to-day that 6| cents per hundred dollar value is the rate from the head of the lakes to Buffalo, where formerly it was 30 cents for a hundred dollars. That makes quite a difference. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) thinks that if we repealed the coastal laws we would have no merchant marine left. If one studies the report of the royal commission appointed to inquire into the lake freight rates on grain and insurance, he will find that these Great Lakes shippers are making a great deal of profit. Page 36 of the report deals with the Great Lakes Transportation Company, and the commission makes some rather interesting deductions. The company has shown 11 per cent as the actual return on their investment. Now the deductions of the commission would show that it was actually about 45 per cent.
What company was that?
The Great Lakes Transportation Company. They value one vessel at $525,000, and the commission values it at $125,860.
What is the capacity of the vessel?

I do not think they
give the capacity. The Mathews Steamship Company show an accounting of 10-24 per cent and in connection with this company

the commission quote a letter that was issued by Mr. Mathews, the manager, on August 20th, 1922, as follows:
The average annual net earnings derived from operation, after depreciation and taxes for the five years ending January 31, 1922, amounted to almost five times the total interest charges on the bonds now outstanding including the present issue. Preliminary figures for the first half of the year 1922, indicate that the earnings for this year may be considerably in excess of the above proportion.
The commission goes on to report:
The bond issue was $700,000; the interest on that would be $49,000. Five times that would be $245,000; but in exhibit 277 the company claims that its operations for the year 1922 up to the first of September resulted in a loss of $29 709.61.
It is quite apparent from those figures that their supposed earnings of 10.24 per cent are a long way from being correct; the figures would show they are making very substantial profits, and I think there is very little danger indeed of our losing our Canadian Merchant Marine through the repeal of the coastal laws.

Can the minister tell me
if Mr. George Hill is still the superintendent
at Calgary?

Mr. George Hill was suspended, but has been reinstated. The matter was investigated. The reason of the suspension was that he wrote a letter to a gentleman in Alberta that I did not think was a proper letter for him to send out. The matter was investigated, and he has been reinstated. I will read a portion of the letter so that the House may have some idea of the reason for his suspension for a time. It was addressed to Mr. M. G. Gudlangson, and reads:
When my duties call upon me to answer such correspondence as you send me, t/hen I will quit of my own accord. Were I to tell you that my grading was no poorer than Winnipeg, you no doubt will not believe it, nor could you understand if I was to explain. I was raised on a farm and never saw the 'lights of a city until I was over eighteen years old. I used to accumulate a grouch like yours on the farm, because I had to spend my hours when not at school cleaning out the cowsheds and pigpens.
That letter was forwarded to me by the gentleman who received it. I immediately looked into the matter and found that Mr. Gudlangson had written to Mr. Hill and myself upon the same date. I replied to Mr. Gud-langson's letter. Mr. Gudlangson wrote three letters to Mr. Hill. To the first one Mr. Hill paid no attention. He wrcfte another letter and Mr. Hill paid no attention to it. When he wrote a third letter Mr. Hill con-

Supply-Canada Grain Act
descended to answer him by the letter I have read. I felt that any man who would write such a letter to any citizen in Alberta or any other province should be suspended at once. I ordered an investigation, and the matter was investigated. The chairman of the Canada Grain Board reported to me and gave reasons why Mr. Hill had answered in such a manner. He stated that he was working under high tension and a nervous strain.
I replied to him that many men are working under high tension or high strain but they find opportunities to answer letters in a courteous and civil manner. I was informed that Mr. Hill regretted his action very much; so I told them to give Mr. Hill another trial.

Out of what vote will
the expenses of the Royal Grain Commission be paid?

There was a vote last year
which has not covered the expenses, and an amount will be placed in the supplementary estimates to provide for it.

Are there any
grain hospitals at the foot of the lakes?
I cannot answer that question.

Has the minister
any information as to the amount of grain lost at the foot of the lakes?
We have no knowledge of any losses; any losses that occurred would be through private elevators.

I want to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Port William and Rainy River a little while ago so that the correction will appear in the same Hansard that reports his remarks. He was quoting the overages of the United Grain Growers in certain years taking the figures from the Price Waterhouse report. The hon. member is very well versed in some things but he has yet something to learn about the grain trade. He gave certain figures purporting to be the number of bushels of overages which this company had in certain years but in looking up the report I find that the amounts he quoted were the proceeds of the overages in those years. So that those who read Hansard may have some other overages to compare with the figures quoted by the hon. member, I want to quote the figures in regard to one other company in the same year, the Empire and Thunder Bay. In 1912 their overages amounted to 160,821; in 1913, 169,622; in 1914, 59,066; in 1915, 236,223; in 1916-17, 309,643.
I might further point out that in the five years covered by this report the total overages of the elevators under supervision showed a total receipt of $5,304,367. I would quote more figures but the hour is late. I should also like to say something regarding the coastal shipping law, but I may bring it up under the other vote. I will defer my remarks.

Item agreed to.
Dominion Bureau of Statistics, including 6th Census, $200,000.
Surely the minister, having got through a vote of a million dollars does not wish to go further at midnight? How can we stand this day after day?

We have wasted considerable
time discussing something at present under investigation by a royal commission, and I do want to get one or two items through.
The main item is through.

In regard to the minister's
remark, if the House were assured of an opportunity of discussing this question when the report of that commission is submitted, thi3 discussion need not have taken place. But this is the only opportunity we have of taking up the matter.

What can we discuss if
we are to keep away from, the things that are before royal commissions?

The door has been left wide
open for the discussion of everything that does not relate to this particular item. All the other items that will be voted at a later date were discussed in connection with this vote and I raised no objection.

I am sorry the minister
thinks we have wasted a lot of valuable time; I think we have made good use of the evening and have secured a good deal of information.
Why has the minister reduced the expenditure under this item? I believe that the expenditure on the Bureau of Statistics is one outlay which can be justified; this is money well spent.

The decreases are in the staff
and in the completion of the census. A number of machines have been installed that do the work otherwise performed by in-
Supply-Canada Grain Act

d'ividuals. There are also about 20 unnecessary publications issued monthly including preliminary bulletins the elimination of which will represent no loss.

You do not contemplate
cutting down the service?

No. Let me give my hon.
friend the benefit of an investigation I made myself. I had a letter from a friend who wished to have a certain person in the department re-classified. On investigation I found that this gentleman had under his charge some 12 employees. I made an examination of the work carried on by that particular branch, and having some little knowledge of what a stenographer or an office hand should be able to do I decided that instead of recommending an increase in the salary of the gentleman in charge of the office there should be immediately dispensed with the services of 5 out of the 12 persons under him. I thought that 7 would be able to carry on the work efficiently and satisfactorily.

I will certainly support
the minister in any contraction he may make and I hope he will pursue the good work further. I will give him a hint now as to what he might do by association with his colleagues. We made a persistent eflort to get all statistical work concentrated in the one service;
I thought it was practically complete and successful. I find now that there are statistics branches almost everywhere; I do not know whether new ones have grown up or whether this is a revival of the old ones. For example, there is a statistics branch in the Labour department. What in the world is the need of that? The statistics should all be in one office, and then there could be economy as well as efficiency. Let me give the minister an illustration. I got from a business man just lately a letter in which he refers to some correspondence with the statistics end of the Labour department. This business man had given out certain facts in his own literature, and important and interesting they were. They had reached the Labour department. The Labour department statistics office wrote and asked where these statistics had been secured; they would very much like to have them. He wrote back informing them that he got the figures from the Statistics branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Here was one government department writing to a business man to find out where information was secured that came from

another government department just across the road! What is the common sense of maintaining those two offices, especially when one does not know what the other is doing? Had I known this matter was coming up I would have brought the correspondence down it is really laughable. Let the minister have a talk with his absent colleague, the -Minister of Labour, to see if he cannot close up the factory there and use one central statistics office.

I quite agree with the right
hon. leadter of the opposition that there are many branches in various departments that might well be combined. But he knows that it is a condition which we inherited-I am not finding any fault with that-
I think you have developed it.

-but I hope that during the
time we are in office we will be able to remedy this condition.
It is getting worse.
I do not think so.
What power or authority can the chief statistician exercise to secure statistics from the various departments?

I am sure that would be a
very simple matter to work out. The Statistics Act covers the duties of the bureau and additional services may be assigned to it, from time to time.

Has he any authority to
demand statistics from the departments? I understand that he has not. I should like to know.

Arrangements can be made to
provide for co-ordination.

Some time ago I asked for
statistics from the Bureau of Statistics, and was told I could only get the information from another department.
I suppose there are some instances like that to which my right hon. friend referred.
I have never got the information yet.
Well, if you ask our department you will at least receive a reply.

The minister should not have said that he inherited the condition.

Questions
The whole unification from beginning to end took place under the late government; there was no chief statistician before. Now, I do not say that in the Labour department there was not perhaps some relic left.

I am sure my right hon. friend
is not objecting to the chief statistician?

No, I am not; he is one of the best officials any government ever had. But I am inclined to the belief that there is growing up a sort of second crop in the various departments, and why an the world there need be, especially in the Labour department, I am at a loss to understand. If there is not power in the chief statistician to get data from the other departments, there certainty should be. I was under the impression that he possessed such power.

I quite agree with my right
hon. friend that there should not be duplication in the other departments.

I want to direct the attention
of the minister-perhaps he has already had the matter under his observation-to the report of the Haldane Commission in Great Britain some three or four years ago with regard to the reconstruction of the ministry, m which the essential and vital importance . of statistical work is outlined and a procedure is suggested by which it can be made a really effective and centralized function of government.
Item agreed to.
